title: 病毒式游戏混搭：AI 反编译能力对游戏意味着什么
content:
Viral Game Mash-ups: What AI Decompilation Capabilities Mean For Games
Skip to content
AI x Gaming
Viral Game Mash-ups: What AI Decompilation Capabilities Mean For Games
By Francois Courset •   October 13, 2026
Source: Naavik
If you’ve spent any time on social media over the past two weeks, you’ve probably seen some crazy game mash-ups: a
Modern Warfare operator landing a kickflip
, a
Minecraft creeper wandering the streets of Night City
, or
Mario fighting against Elden Ring bosses
. These viral mash-ups racking up millions of views are coming from amateur coders who are using AI tools to decompile commercial games and stitch together characters and mechanics into playable Frankenstein experiences.
On the surface, it’s pure internet chaos. But behind the absurdity, these mods highlight some vertiginous implications for the future of games, and pretty much any software development. What happens when the barriers that used to protect source code start falling apart, with AI tools now able to reverse-engineer entire games? Let’s dig into what this new trend means, the technology behind it, and the implications for game studios.
How Did This Remix Trend Take Root? And Why Now?
To start, it’s worth noting that this trend has largely taken off on
X
, where users have been sharing short clips of their latest mash-up experiments.
A skateboarding feature added to Modern Warfare
pulled in 7.4M views, while
a mod turning Minecraft into Elden Ring
hit a staggering 23.3M. Further down the rabbit hole, we’ve seen
monstrosities fusing multiple games together
, from Mario 64 to Portal.
Source:
X
Many of these are rough prototypes, some are outright broken, and some are not even available to play. But dismissing them would be a mistake. The capabilities are broad (merging characters, gameplay loops, and beyond), and they’re accessible. Pretty much anyone with limited technical knowledge can take a swing using a simple AI prompt.
The game remixing trend quickly expanded beyond mash-ups.
Users have rebuilt P.T. entirely
, a PS4 game created by Kojima and originally released by Konami, making it natively playable on PC and positioning it as a game preservation initiative.
Another user made GTA V playable in browser
, yet another made a native port of
Bloodborne on PC
, fully bypassing PlayStation’s historic walled gardens.
The trend has been fueled by a clear technical inflection point. First came GPT Astra in early September, which blew past competing models on the
SRE benchmark
, the go-to measure of a model’s ability to reverse-engineer software. Then, in late September, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 lowered the cost of entry with cheaper tokens and sharper coding performance. It has become the model that mash-up creators most often say they rely on.
Source:
SRE Benchmark Leaderboard
To further understand this technical unlock, it helps to step back and look at how games, and really most software, reach players in the first place. What a consumer downloads is never the game’s source code. It is a binary, the output of
a process called compilation
, which machines can execute easily but humans struggle to read. Think of source code as the recipe, the human-readable instructions developers write, and compilation as the baking that turns those instructions into something a computer can execute. Decompiling is like tasting a cake and trying to reverse-engineer a recipe that gets you the same result. It is possible, but historically it has been hard, slow, and expensive.
Source:
YouTube
What the latest AI models do is radically accelerate the decompilation process. An agent drafts a plausible version of a function by analyzing the binary. The system then recompiles it with the original compiler and compares the resulting machine code byte by byte against the original. It then repeats the process until it finds a perfect match.
AI doesn’t change the method so much as it industrializes it: since most functions can be solved independently, multiple agents can run in parallel, turning years of effort into a matter of days. Ultimately, this erodes the protection between a shipped product and its source code.
This website
tracking game decompilation progress, which was previously driven by human effort, had marked 13 games as “Decomps” complete before September; since then, 24 more have already been completed. However, a full decompilation remains a tedious process.
Maurice Heumann
, who decompiled Modern Warfare 2 using Claude, reports using up to 17 agents and 235B tokens over 11 weeks.
From Decompilation to Pass-Through Remix and Game Ports
These emerging initiatives don’t rely solely on full decompilation; instead, they use a range of techniques. We recommend
this video
for a detailed overview, but in short, users rely on three main techniques:
Pass-through mods:
These mods don’t need to rebuild a game from the ground up. Instead, they translate actions and physics from one title into another. Think of a pass-through mod as a live interpreter sitting between two games running at the same time: it watches what happens in one and instructs the other to perform a matching action. Tools such as
Universal Modder
and
Reverse Engineer Anything
(REA) give Claude the ability to create pass-through mods end to end, including a dedicated “mashup-mods” skill. Both grew quickly in popularity, reaching 5.8K and 32.8K stars on GitHub, respectively, in just a handful of days.
Source:
YouTube
Porting mechanics:
Rather than decompiling a full game, AI can isolate specific mechanics (
Mirror’s Edge’s parkour
, a skateboarding game’s physics, etc.) and rebuild them inside an entirely different title, like Skyrim or Modern Warfare. Rather than running the original game in parallel, as pass-through approaches do, the destination game reproduces the behavior on its own. This approach is far more versatile, particularly for teams trying to understand what makes a competitor’s game tick and then replicate, remix, or improve on it in the
